query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of Al additions to promote short-range ordering (SRO) in the NbMoTaW high-entropy alloy can improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy NbMoTaW with poor room-temperature ductility
generation.intervention: Introduction of Al additions to promote SRO
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic driver for ordering, which directly corroborates experimental findings that Al additions promote SRO
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature ductility without compromising high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance
generation.boundary: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW composition, SRO promotion through Al additions
generation.uncertainty: Extent and underlying causes of ordering, impact of SRO on mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: Experimental investigation of the effect of Al additions on SRO and mechanical properties of NbMoTaW
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of Al additions does not promote SRO or improve room-temperature ductility, the hypothesis is falsified

Body
Mechanical properties of single-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs) can be unusually enhanced than many conventional single-phase engineering alloys (). Recent computational and experimental studies indicate that the atomic distribution in such solid solution HEAs may not be completely random as originally believed, but exhibit localized pockets of nonrandom distributions, also called “clustered ordering” (). While strengthening due to such local chemical clusters has been reported in Al (), Ni (), Fe () base alloys, and more recently, in complex bulk metallic glasses () and HEAs (, ), the ability to systematically engineer its nature and extent has so far eluded us.
While the quinary CoCrFeNiMn, arguably the most extensively studied HEA, has been established as a single-phase alloy (), local chemical ordering was recently experimentally shown, and computationally validated, in its “subset” ternary CoCrNi alloy (, ) Similarly, direct experimental evidence of nonrandom atomic distributions has been presented in CoCrFeNiPd () and CoNiV () HEAs. To overcome the prohibitive computational costs of very large supercells in DFT calculations, we generated both 108-atom and 216-atom special quasirandom structures (SQSs) (, ) to model the FCC Al0.27CoFeNi alloy with SRO. As shown in SI Appendix, Table S3, the pair correlation functions of our SQSs agree well with those of the short-range ordered alloy predicted by our MC simulations. For comparison, SQSs for the completely random Al0.27CoFeNi alloy were also created to closely reproduce the pair correlation functions of the random alloy (SI Appendix, Table S4). The pair distribution functions of the random and SRO Al0.27CoFeNi alloy are shown in Fig. 2 E and F, respectively. Our DFT calculations with 216 (108)-atom SQSs indicate that, at 1200°C, SRO can reduce the total energy of the Al0.27CoFeNi alloy by 0.118 (0.200) eV per Al atom. Thus, our simple 1NN bond energy model used in MC simulations remarkably predicts the energy reduction due to SRO to be 0.208 eV per Al atom, which falls in the range predicted by our DFT-SQS calculations.
